title: Fudge Finds a Friend
markdown:
The toy box was a cozy place. Toys waited there, soft and warm, for little hands. This afternoon, sunbeams painted sleepy stripes across the velvety lining. Fudge the ferret, fur as soft as a whispered secret, nestled near his little red train. It had three carriages that loved to roll along imaginary tracks. Shush-shush, they went, and that sound made Fudge feel content. Beside him Clover the calf lay with her head on a plump pillow that smelled faintly of lavender. Her eyes were as deep as a quiet morning meadow.

Fudge’s whiskers twitched. He nudged the train. The paint felt smooth.

“My little train is ready for a friend,” he murmured. “A passenger. In the first carriage. Today we will find one.”

He loved imagining journeys. With a passenger, the journeys would be even nicer. A tiny warm flutter lived in his tummy. If the first seat stayed empty, the best part of the afternoon would be missed.

Clover gave a gentle moo, like soft bells. That was enough. Fudge’s tail flicked, a small happy flag.

“We must look,” he said.

They left their sunny spot and moved toward the deeper, quieter corners of the toy box. They did not visit those corners often. Shadows stretched a little longer there. The familiar smell of playdough mixed with paper and dried flowers, like old storybooks taking a nap.

They wiggled past a tower of soft colourful blocks, rounded like gentle giants. Fudge sniffed the spaces between. A marble winked and rolled away, too round, too ready to escape a carriage. They tiptoed around a pile of plush animals, button eyes watching, fur inviting. A ribbon lay in a sleepy curl. Pretty. Not a passenger.

“Where could you be?” Fudge whispered to the empty seat.

They passed a tiny tea set. The cups were empty and very fine. Clover sniffed the lavender pillow-smell that had followed them, and shook her head. Not here.

On a high shelf sat a wise old teddy, Berwyn, his stuffing a little lopsided with age. Fudge’s whiskers brushed worn fur.

“Berwyn,” Fudge asked, “have you seen a passenger for my little red train?”

Berwyn blinked one button eye, slow.

“Hmm,” he rumbled, like the creak of old furniture. “Look for something small. Something quiet. Something that likes to rest and dream.”

Fudge felt a tiny wobble in his knees. What if they could not find the friend? What if the train had to wait? For a moment he wished for the sunny spot again, where everything was known.

Clover nudged him with her soft nose, warm and sure. “We will find our friend, Fudge.”

He remembered: small, quiet, likes to rest. They looked in a mitten that had lost its pair. Warm. Empty. They looked behind a picture book whose pages smelled like dust and apples. A pressed flower. No friend. Then Fudge peered into a woolen nest woven from loose yarn, like a warm hug. And there, nestled in the fluff, was something round and smooth and grey.

A button.

The perfect size for the little train’s seat. A gentle grey orb. It was Mr Buttons, so shy and so sleepy that he had settled down for a nap in the softest quietest place he could find.

Fudge looked. He had imagined a friend who would make the train sing with fun. Mr Buttons was so still. So peaceful. A little shiver — what if this quiet passenger meant the train would always be slow? He pictured lively adventures. Letting that picture go felt like a tiny ache.

Then he felt Clover’s nearness, and the cool smooth button under his whiskers. He took a breath. He sighed, soft as letting go of a balloon, and nudged Mr Buttons. The button rolled a little and did not roll away.

He did not need a bustling friend today. He needed this sleepy one. The lively wish floated off like a dandelion seed. What remained was a grey moon waiting for a red sky.

Together they guided Mr Buttons toward the little red train, past the blocks and the lopsided teddy shelf, back toward the sunbeam stripes. Fudge’s nimble paws settled him in the first carriage. He fit. Snug. Like a little grey moon in a red sky. Fudge pushed the train along the soft lining. Not shush-shush this time. A muffled roll-roll. A whisper of movement. The carriages followed, polite and slow. Clover walked beside, hooves silent on velvet.

Fudge looked at Clover. His eyes held a new calm. The train was complete. Not loud. Content. Ready for peaceful journeys through a land of dreams, where the air stayed soft and the light stayed gentle, and the first carriage no longer waited empty in the sun.

As Fudge drifted toward sleep, sunbeams thinning to evening, he heard the roll-roll. Clover’s lavender pillow rose and fell. Mr Buttons sat in the first carriage, not singing, not bouncing, only riding. The old flutter was only a breeze now. Fudge’s whiskers twitched with peace, and he dreamed of moonlit tracks, and a small grey passenger who liked to rest.
